title: The Overdraft That Never Goes Back to Zero
linkedin:
Most overdrafts start for a specific reason. A wage run before an invoice clears, a stock order before a seasonal peak, a tax instalment in an awkward month.

The plan is always to pay it back to zero once the cash catches up.

The problem is the next inconvenient month usually arrives before the last one is fully repaid. The balance never quite gets back to where it started.

Eighteen months later, a facility approved as short-term cover has quietly become permanent debt, still priced and structured like it's temporary.

The number worth watching isn't the limit. It's the lowest balance the account touches over a rolling twelve months. That floor is no longer working capital, it's core capital sitting inside an account priced for short-term swings, at a rate well above what a term facility would cost for the same money.

Most owners only find this out when the bank's annual review raises it first, often with a reduced limit or tighter conditions attached.

The fix isn't removing the overdraft. It's splitting the floor balance into a properly priced term facility and leaving a smaller revolving facility for genuine seasonal swings, which is exactly what an overdraft is built for.

Many Brisbane and Queensland business owners carry a business overdraft that never quite gets back to zero, and it's worth checking whether that's happening in your own accounts. It usually starts for a good reason, a wage run before a big invoice clears, a stock order ahead of a busy season, or a tax instalment in an awkward month. The facility gets drawn down, the pressure eases, and the plan is to repay it once the cash catches up.

The trouble is the next inconvenient month often arrives before the last one is fully repaid, so the balance never quite returns to where it started. Over a year or two, a facility that was approved as short-term cover can quietly become permanent debt, still priced at overdraft rates that are usually well above what an equivalent term loan would cost for the same money.

The fix isn't to remove the overdraft. It's to look at the lowest balance the account has touched over the past twelve months, work out how much of that is genuinely permanent capital, and move that portion into a facility priced and structured for its actual purpose, leaving a smaller overdraft for real seasonal swings.
